en: Jeljetpes went out to his people.
Finishing the people’s business,
Jeljetpes set out to depart,
What remedy is there for this strange affair?
Jeljetpes went out after his elder,
Toward his Kyrgyz people,
Jeljetpes set out to find them,
Having seen humiliation and hardship,
Jeljetpes said he would see it,
Driving the herds this way,
Jeljetpes said he would see it.
Hear of all the champions,
The khan’s wrath will be unleashed,
Seeing the place of death,
The gray day drove the mount onward.
Mounted on a lean yellow horse,
The poor hero, unable to reach him,
Cried in anguish and rode hard,
The wrathful khagan who roamed,
Leading those who obeyed,
The corrupt eye saw it,
Let us sink into the earth.
Having gone and returned,
“Let us enter elsewhere.”
Thus spoke Jeljetpes,
Making it known to the heroes,
Bringing the boys to obey his words,
Providing sustenance for his people’s hearts,
Jeljetpes intended to ensnare them.
From Chyngteñir’s net,
From the hand of the wrathful day,
Jeljetpes was about to remain.
Before the sign of the sun arose,
Such a stern and imposing hero,
The accomplished champion Jeljetpes,
“If we leave together, you have seen it,” he said,
There was no movement and no quarrel,
“Simply take warning from me,” he said,
I came with the horse lathered and spent,
Jeljetpes prevailed over all of you,
“I will recover your due,” he said,
Without sitting and without ceasing to move,
“Remain where you understand,” he said,
Khan Bangyr said this,
He told of the dreadful hardship he had seen,
After the man departed again,
Jeljetpes entered upon the road.
The one he led was a heroic champion,
His breast was full of deep sorrow,
Toward the churned dust,
The ill-starred wanderer was to come.
Chyngteñir, who traveled with thousands,
From the snare laid over these people,
Had saved a man without entanglement.
Thus spoke Jeljetpes,
With a message carried in honor,
Sitting down, he put on his coat,
He set on his cap and mounted his horse,
He took the road toward the khan’s camp.
Where would a hero ever shrink back?
The gleaming Ala-Too,
The eye travels across the green plain,
Was it a land from which none would draw back?
Pitching such a firm encampment,
The camp of forty countless ranks,
Was this a land that would bear such a load?
Its crimson market-stalls,
Was this a land one would not visit?
Its masters were a broad and numerous people,
They were a blessed people,
Their nets were spread freely,
They were said to be a most prosperous people,
He bound them, intending to cut them down.
The hurried one dwelt in the open country,
Let his tree not go there,
They called it a blessed people.
Jeljetpes saw this,
There was no straight path where he roamed,
Jeljetpes of paradise-bright eyes,
If this wrathful boar attacks,
“What kind of brute is he?” I said,
The merciless boar,
At noon he fell into their hands,
Wondering what remedy there could be,
Cast many sheep upon the white ground,
His swelling grief was ruined,
He went once to see the livestock,
All saw the Kyrgyz people,
They would remain at the place of slaughter,
He went once after seeing their lives,
They were a people from the lesser side,
May God cover them abundantly like snow,
He spoke to his people as a mortal.
“Strike and drive them,” said this one,
A Chinese khan with no preparation or khanly order,
They were a merciless people,
Living until the fire was kindled,
Until wisdom closed its eyes,
Until then this people would live,
Wondering what would happen then,
Only a little of the plain remained,
Until he had settled this in his mind,
Until he had fully explained himself,
Until he sent word to the people,
May God’s command not show such a fate,
He appeared toward Ebegey,
What the wise among the people knew,
He had seen night here before,
He had seen the hardest trial of all.
The Kyrgyz son of the people,
Saw something immeasurable,
A star stirred in the sky,
With the hero Kenen the destroyer,
He became a close companion in plunder,
Settling in Talas, he became a friend,
He became a hero to the white-kalpak people,
Keeping the horde, he became khan,
Honor the two tribes,
He was a truly wise soul.
For Kenen beyond measure,
A gray felt mat became a throne.
With wisdom, suffering, and hardship,
Joined together with the one who broke through,
Entwined with his kinsmen,
In the horde that stood aroused,
Though he was a Kyrgyz among strangers,
Without merely watching and failing to act,
This was a blessed deed and word,
Ebegey, the wise Chinese man,
The twins he led,
A boundless road remained,
Taking provisions and a flask,
Taking the two heroes in hand,
“Give us the people we seek.”
With a lion’s strike and tiger’s strength,
They came out on the hunt,
Driving Kuman and shooting,
As the sun sank red,
Drawing fire through their labor,
They went to the Kyrgyz heroes,
Let him reckon the people’s scattered condition,
Let him see and inspect with his own eyes,
The son of hero Kenen,
My Tengir who overturns the world,
The people’s grievance against their friends,
The binding at his waist.
His covering that would not freeze in the cold,
Your mighty protector in whom you took refuge,
The warrior, gray-maned hero Kenen,
From God the Almighty,
The protector you obtained through prayer,
Your two lion-like champions,
The two had arrived,
Ebegey and Kogoy, my two elders,
Before the two elders,
With formidable swords strapped on,
Like clouds about to bring hail,
Their faces turned fierce,
The dream I saw was a fortunate dream,
A dream in which anguish struck the heart,
A dream in which the people fell into distress,
Ebegey and Kogoy, my two elders,
A dream of going to the true world beyond,
The dear Kyrgyz people in their white kalpaks,
A dream in which they fell into calamity.”
Whatever fate may be, we shall see it,
If the famed rumor is true,
The command of my Creator,
Thick-armed and stone-hearted,
We shall see what comes from the enemy’s wealth.
In the dream I was seeing,
That notch lay carved out,
As that harsh age passes over us,
The sunlit world passes from our hearts,
Those left among the many souls,
What will become of us?
Unable to advance freely into the struggle,
It seems we shall be made worthless.
Your strength will go to waste,
What will become of us?
With our outstretched legs unable to draw in,
It seems we shall become corpses.
Without looking back when our backs are galled,
Encountering an enemy,
It seems we shall be smothered.
Living on after being told to flee,
Drinking water in an unknown land,
Embracing and kissing the child,
Stretched out and halted upon the earth,
It seems we shall become mere game.
The torment of this world,
It seems we shall endure and see it.
With nothing left and no darkness remaining,
The fire-eater made himself known,
The Kyrgyz host seemed as old as an age,
The age itself seemed countless,
Like the eighteen thousand worlds,
The one burned and left in history,
Putting on a sheltering coat,
When his servant struck the khan,
He pressed forward with sheer force.
Ebegey and Köböy, the two of you,
Kenen, the hero left standing,
The champion presented by the padishah,
The fire that burned everything,
No safe refuge can be found,
Compare it with the whole world.
There is no such wonder in the three worlds,
Kertulpar and Kermekash,

What knowledge is this?
This is the division from the twin companions.
Listen to these words of mine,
Their strength accomplished it.
This land is Ala-Too,
Its days were like mountains,
The nights of those days were cold waters.
Since Ala-Too became this way,
Since it fell into suffering and prison,
This is the hardship of the world,
Alas, that he turned away.
Let the two lions return home,
God knows the days,
God knows the world,
They lived on safely without dying.
One became afraid of death,
Weeping before hardship,
He became iron-hearted,
No hero remained to break and slaughter,
No world stands alongside it,
The account of what was made,
When it comes upon us, we shall see it,
If a hostile man comes, we shall strike him.
However much delight and hell,
If it is written like beads, we shall see it.
Created as a strange boar,
We shall see it with the truth.
Ebegey and Köböy said this,
The twin lion-like boys
They sent out upon the road.
That day the two heroes lay down,
Propped on their elbows, they slept,
Dozing awhile, they rested,
Without pulling against one another,
Without stirring their work,
They sank into heavy sleep.
This world was uncertain,
They lay without receiving news.
The sun rose encircling the mountain,
Forty days before it emerged,
When the freezing season came,
They roused the embers from the cave.
They performed the appointed prayer,
They rose from the double enclosure,
Preparing their weapons and gear,
